hook.support: Your boss won’t pay you. Your phone broke a week after you bought it. Someone posted a photo of you. Who do you call? There’s a right place for each one. And it’s usually free.
hook.core: Your boss hasn’t paid you for two shifts. A shop won’t fix the phone that broke after a week. Someone posted a private photo of you. Each problem has a right place to go, often free, but most people don’t know where to start. Asking the wrong place wastes days.
hook.extend: Unpaid wages, a faulty product, online abuse, a bond that won’t come back. Australia has an agency or service for almost every problem, and most are free. The hard part is knowing which one, and telling a reliable service from a dodgy website that only looks official.

why.support: Knowing who helps saves time and stress. It also helps you help your friends and family.
why.core: Knowing who to ask saves time, money and stress. It’s also how you help a mate or a family member who’s stuck.
why.extend: Finding and checking the right agency is part of running your own life. It’s also one of the most useful things you can do for someone else who is stuck.

articles.title: The right place to ask

body.support:
Most problems have a place that helps. Most are **free**.

**The Australian Government** helps with:
- pay and work rights: **Fair Work Ombudsman**.
- tax: **ATO**.
- Medicare and Centrelink: **Services Australia**.
- online bullying: **eSafety Commissioner**.

**The Victorian Government** helps with:
- your licence: **Transport Victoria**.
- renting and shopping problems: **Consumer Affairs Victoria**.
- police and schools.

**Your local council** helps with parks, libraries, footpaths and youth services.

**Community services** are not run by the government. **headspace**, **Kids Helpline** and **Lifeline** help with mental health.

Before you trust a website, check:
1. Who runs it?
2. Is it free?
3. Does it have a real phone number or address?
4. Is it up to date?
body.core:
For most problems, there’s a right place to go, and it’s often **free**. Australia has three levels of government, plus community services.

**The Australian Government** (federal) looks after things for the whole country:
- pay and work rights: **Fair Work Ombudsman**.
- tax and your tax file number: **Australian Taxation Office (ATO)**.
- Medicare and Centrelink: **Services Australia**.
- serious online bullying or image abuse: **eSafety Commissioner**.
- scams: **Scamwatch**.

**The Victorian Government** (state) looks after:
- licences and transport: **Transport Victoria**.
- renting, bonds and faulty products: **Consumer Affairs Victoria**.
- police, public schools, TAFE and hospitals.

**Your local council** looks after your area: parks, libraries, footpaths, bins, and youth services and programs.

**Community (non-government) services** are run by charities and not-for-profits: **headspace** (mental health, ages 12 to 25), **Kids Helpline**, **Lifeline**, free legal centres, and finders like **Ask Izzy**.

Before you trust a service or website, check four things:
1. **Who runs it?** Government sites end in **.gov.au**. Charities explain who they are on an “About us” page.
2. **Is it free?** Real help services usually are.
3. **Real contact details?** A phone number, opening hours, an address.
4. **Up to date?** Look for recent dates.
.
Then read the service’s page for the key facts: what they help with, who can use it, and how to contact them.
body.extend:
For most problems, there is an agency or service set up to help, and many are **free**. Knowing which level is in charge saves days of being passed around.

**The Australian Government** (federal) handles national matters. Think pay and rights at work (**Fair Work Ombudsman**), tax (**ATO**), Medicare and Centrelink (**Services Australia**), serious online abuse (**eSafety Commissioner**) and scams (**Scamwatch**).

**The Victorian Government** (state) handles licences and transport (**Transport Victoria**), and renting, bonds and problems with things you buy (**Consumer Affairs Victoria**). It also runs police, public schools, TAFE and hospitals.

**Local councils** handle your local area: parks, libraries, footpaths, bins and youth programs.

**Non-government organisations** fill many gaps. Examples are **headspace** (mental health, ages 12–25), **Kids Helpline**, **Lifeline**, free legal centres, and finders such as **Ask Izzy**. Many get some government money but run themselves.

Copycat sites sometimes look official, so check four things.
1. **Who runs it?** Government sites end in **.gov.au**. Real charities explain who runs them and who funds them.
2. **Cost.** Real help services are usually free. A fee to “help” with a free government process is a red flag.
3. **Contact details.** Look for a real phone number, hours and address.
4. **Up to date.** Look for recent dates.
.
Then skim the service’s page. Find what it does, who is eligible, what it costs and how to contact it. Note what you’ll need to have ready.

caseStudies.title: Ask Izzy: help, found fast

body.support:
When you have nowhere to sleep, finding help is hard. You might not have much phone credit. You might not know where to look.

In **2016**, a charity called **Infoxchange** launched **Ask Izzy**. It’s a free website. It helps people find a bed, a meal, money help or a counsellor near them.

It lists more than **350,000** services across Australia.

It was built with help from people who had been homeless. They knew what was hard.

You don’t need to give your name to use it.
body.core:
When someone has nowhere to sleep, finding help can feel impossible. They might have little phone data, no computer and no idea which service to call.

In January **2016**, a not-for-profit called **Infoxchange** launched **Ask Izzy**. It’s a free website for your phone. It helps people find services nearby: a bed, meals, money help, family violence support, counselling and more. Google and other big companies helped build it. The Prime Minister at the time, Malcolm Turnbull, launched it.

Ask Izzy lists more than **350,000** services across Australia. People who had been homeless helped design it, along with the workers who support them. So it works the way they need it to. In its first weeks, it had more than **200,000** searches.

You don’t need to give your name to use it.
body.extend:
Finding help is hardest for the people who need it most. Someone sleeping rough may have little data, an old phone and no idea which of dozens of services to try.

In January **2016**, the not-for-profit **Infoxchange** launched **Ask Izzy**. It’s a free, anonymous website for phones. It lists more than **350,000** services across Australia, from housing and meals to money help, family violence support and counselling. Partners included Google, REA Group and News Corp Australia. The Prime Minister at the time, Malcolm Turnbull, launched it.

Most importantly, it was **co-designed** with people who had been homeless and the workers who support them. Within its first weeks, it recorded more than **200,000** searches.

Ask Izzy shows that good information only helps if people can find and use it. The people who need a service are often the best guides to designing it.

source.name: Infoxchange — “Ask Izzy set to bridge the gap for Australia’s homeless” (2016)

model.text:
**Problem:** My boss says my first two shifts were a “trial”, so he won’t pay me for them.

**Who can help:** Fair Work Ombudsman (Australian Government).

**Is it reliable?**
- Who runs it: the Australian Government. Website ends in .gov.au.
- Cost: free.
- Contact: phone 13 13 94, plus an online enquiry form.
- Up to date: the page was updated this year.

**Have ready:** the dates and hours I worked, the business name, and my texts with the boss.

**What I’ll say:** “Hi, I’m 16 and I worked two shifts. My boss says they were a trial and won’t pay me. Should I have been paid?”
why: The problem is written in one clear sentence.
All four reliability checks have real evidence, not just “it looks fine”.
It lists what to have ready and a short opening line, so the call is easy.

teacher.overview: Students learn where help comes from (Australian Government, Victorian Government, local council, community services), match problems to the right agency, check reliability (who runs it, cost, contact details, currency), and read a service page for key information. They build a help map for a real problem and get ready to contact the service. The case study is Ask Izzy, a free directory of 350,000+ services co-designed with people who have experienced homelessness.

Check the school’s web filter allows government and support-service sites.
Have the school wellbeing team’s contact details ready in case a student raises a real concern.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** underpaid — Australia (Fair Work Ombudsman); footpath — council; learner permit test — Victoria (Transport Victoria); feeling low — community (headspace, Kids Helpline); private photo shared — Australia (eSafety Commissioner); faulty phone — Victoria (Consumer Affairs Victoria).

**Annotation:** 1 who runs it (community legal centre, state funded); 2 what they help with; 3 eligibility (12–25, Victoria); 4 cost (free, confidential); 5 contact options and hours; 6 what to have ready, and 000 for emergencies.

**Case study:** beds, meals, money help, family violence support, counselling; people with lived experience know what makes help hard to find; reliable: run by a known not-for-profit, free, clear who built it, widely used.

realityCheck: **Students may raise real, personal problems.** Make it clear they can use a made-up or “a friend might” problem. Follow your school’s wellbeing procedures if a disclosure happens.
**Never ask students to share private problems with the class.** The help map is handed to you, not presented.
**Contacting the service is optional.** Writing what they’d say is enough evidence; some students will want to actually call, which is great.
**School filters sometimes block support sites.** Test the main sites before the lesson.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students are often surprised that most of these services are free, and many share them at home.
